catalog_quote: [Harrison 1977: 154] In Mokilese, a verb phrase with an enclitic or enclitics carries a single primary stress, on the penultimate mora. Thus: ókdek 'to lie prone', okdékda 'to lie back (lit. to lie up)', okdekdáhwe 'to lie back there (at a known place)', okdekdahwéhr 'to lie back there and then' where long vowels count as two morae. [Harrison 1984: 388] Though stress assignment in MOK is a complex matter yet to be explored in detail, it appears that primary stress is usually penultimate, though sometimes initial. ... Further, the fact that #CV reduplication is retained in MOK before a long vowel (for example, doadoahk to work) is explained by the fact that primary stress falls on the long 'root' vowel, where stress is seen as sensitive to vocalic moras rather than to syllables as such. The very tentative nature of these proposals must be borne in mind. [n. 21, p. 398] Rehg (personal communication) has suggested that stress in PNP is realised as a rise in amplitude on the penultimate vowel and of pitch on the antepenultimate. I can neither confirm nor deny a similar pattern in MOK, lacking convincing acoustic data.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. (28 pp., text present). p.14 = printed p.388, sec. 4.1: text reads 'Though stress assignment in MOK is a complex matter yet to be explored in detail, it ap[p]ears that primary stress is usually penultimate, though sometimes initial.21.. Further, the fact that #CV reduplication is retained in MOK before a long vowel (for example, doadoahk to work) is explained by the fact that primary stress falls on the long 'root' vowel, where stress is seen as sensitive to vocalic moras rather than to syllables as such. The very tentative nature of these proposals must be borne in mind.' p.24 = p.398 n.21: 'Rehg (personal communication) has suggested that stress in PNP is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress normally falls on the penultimate mora (long vowels count two morae, so a final long vowel or a long penult vowel attracts stress), which surfaces as penultimate-syllable stress in most words; Harrison notes some words with initial stress and calls the system not yet fully analysed. His 1977 dissertation (p. 154, file) states the rule more sharply: 'In Mokilese, a verb phrase with an enclitic or enclitics carries a single primary stress, on the penultimate mora.. where long vowels count as two morae' (okdek > okdekda > okdekdahwe > okdekdahwehr with stress shifting rightward).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any Harrison source.
new_statements.exceptions: 'sometimes initial' (1984, no examples given synchronically; a reconstructed PMC *manana with initial stress is posited); high vowels may be 'skipped over' by stress placement (1984 p. 393, e.g. ária 'gaff', not *ariá.. scanned-garbled example); author stresses the tentative nature and lack of acoustic data.
new_statements.domain_note: 1984 statement is about word-level primary stress; 1977 statement gives the domain as the verb phrase plus its enclitics (directionals, -ehr etc.), which form one phonological unit with a single primary stress on the penultimate mora. The 1976 reference grammar itself is silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Mokilese (Mokil atoll and the Mokilese community on Pohnpei), glottocode moki1238, ISO mkj; no dialect split involved. Harrison abbreviates it MOK; PNP = Pohnpeian in his footnote.
